DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
## Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Bottom line.** The price increases are reasonable, and the competitor check supports them. But the paper's two headline conclusions don't survive its own data:
- **The mushroom risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest.** It also isn't uniquely the lowest seller: it ties with specials at 90 plates a week.
- **The £42,000 projection ignores the 12% beef price rise from 1 April**, which the paper itself reports. Including it cuts the gain by about a third, and the main-course margin stays at roughly 69% rather than rising to 71%.

### 1. The case for removing the risotto is backwards

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% (lowest) | £15.60 |
| Specials | 64% | — |

By percentage margin, the steak is the weakest dish and the risotto the strongest. In cash per plate, the risotto earns more than the curry and the burger. Section 5.2 and the author's description both state the opposite.

The replacement could also cost money. If the new vegetarian special matches the current specials' 64% margin at £14, it earns about £8.96 a plate against the risotto's £11.20. At 90 plates a week, that's roughly **£200 a week less**. The risotto may also be the main vegetarian option, which matters for group bookings.

There may still be good reasons to change it, such as seasonality, kitchen workload, or freshening the menu. But margin and sales don't support removing it.

### 2. The projection leaves out the beef increase

The £810 a week is calculated correctly: £310 + £260 + £240. But beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices:

| | Weekly |
|---|---|
| Extra revenue from price rises | +£810 |
| Burger: 260 × £0.50 more beef cost | −£131 |
| Steak: 120 × £1.25 more beef cost | −£150 |
| **Net gain** | **≈ £529 (≈ £27,500 a year)** |

So the gain is about £27,500 a year, not £42,000.

**Main-course margin:** I estimate it at about 69% now, assuming specials sell at around £16, since their price isn't given. Including the beef increase, it stays at about **69%** after the changes. The price rises mainly *offset* the beef increase rather than restoring margin. That is still worth doing, but it's not the "71%" in the paper.

**VAT:** UK menu prices include 20% VAT. If the margins and the 67%/70% targets are calculated on prices including VAT, both are overstated. A £1 increase in menu price is only about £0.83 of net revenue, which would bring the net gain down to roughly £400 a week, or £20,500 a year. Check which basis your margin figures use.

### 3. No sensitivity analysis on volumes

"We expect volumes to hold" is the paper's only volume assumption. A simple break-even check helps here. Compared with leaving prices unchanged after the beef rise, each increase still pays if volume falls by less than about:
- **fish and chips: 8%**
- **burger: 9%**
- **steak: 12%**

Those are reasonable cushions, and saying so would make the case stronger.

Two supporting claims are weaker than presented:
- **A loyal customer base doesn't mean customers aren't price-sensitive.** Regular guests are the ones most likely to notice an increase.
- **The 2024 price change "had no visible effect."** It would help to know how large that increase was, and how closely bookings were tracked.

### 4. Other errors

- **The restaurant trades five days, not six.** It opens Wednesday to Sunday, but the recommendation says "six trading days a week." The weekly figures aren't affected, but the owners will notice the inconsistency.
- **"We remain the value option."** All three dishes stay below the midpoint of competitors' prices, which checks out. But none will be the cheapest any more: £17.50 is above £16.95, £16.00 above £15.50, and £28.00 above £27.00. The paper should say "competitively priced" rather than imply you're still the lowest.

### 5. Monitoring against the wrong baseline

Spring trade, including Easter, is usually busier than January and February. Comparing April–May volumes with a January–February baseline could hide a real drop in demand caused by the price rises. Better comparisons:
- **year-on-year:** April–May 2025;
- **dishes without price changes**, such as the curry, as a control.

### What holds up

- The competitor price check is thorough, and the proposed prices are well judged against it.
- The arithmetic in Table 1 and the £810 a week are correct.
- Raising beef dish prices ahead of a known 12% beef cost increase is exactly the right move.
- Planning to monitor sales weekly is good practice. It just needs a better baseline.

### Recommended changes

1. Correct the risotto analysis, and either drop its removal or give a different reason.
2. Include the beef increase: about £27,500 a year in extra gross profit, with the main-course margin staying at about 69%.
3. Confirm whether margins are calculated on prices including or excluding VAT, and restate them if needed.
4. Add the break-even volume figures.
5. Fix "six trading days" to five.
6. Monitor against April–May 2025 and against dishes whose prices aren't changing.

The price increases are worth approving. The risotto change, as the paper argues it, is not.
